Home > Storage > PowerMax and VMAX > White Papers > Implementing Proxmox 9 on Dell PowerMax > Cloning a virtual machine to a new target cluster using SnapVX

Cloning a virtual machine to a new target cluster using SnapVX

  • To clone a virtual machine to another Proxmox cluster with SnapVX, you must account for how Proxmox stores VM metadata. Proxmox keeps the virtual disks on shared storage, but it stores each VM’s definition file (.conf) in /etc/pve/qemu-server on the cluster. Even though /etc/pve uses pmxcfs which is a clustered file system, the qemu-server content remains node-specific. Because of that separation, a SnapVX copy of the LVM volume captures the virtual disks but not the VM configuration files required to register and run the VM on the target cluster. This example solves that problem by mounting a small PowerMax NFS share in Figure 90 to both Proxmox clusters and setting the Content to Snippets. This content type supports text-based VM configuration files.

    Figure 90.    NFS for VM configuration files

    Prior to taking the LVM SnapVX snapshot, copy the VM configuration files for that LVM to the NFS share. This may require accessing multiple nodes in the cluster depending on the location of the LVM VMs. Issue a copy of the .conf to the NFS:

    root@pmax172:/etc/pve/qemu-server# cp 101.conf /mnt/pve/vm-confs/snippets/

    You only need to copy the VMs you plan on restoring on the target cluster. Once this is complete, proceed with the snapshot steps that follow. Note this section explains only one method by which you can restore a SnapVX snapshot of a source Proxmox LVM to a different target cluster.

    Step 1

    Take a snapshot of the storage group containing the LVM device. If your storage group has multiple devices and you only wish to snapshot one, there are two options:

    • Use Solutions Enabler and provide the single device.

    dsib2028:~ # symsnapvx est -dev 1D6 -sid 2165 -name single-dev-snap -nop

    Establish operation execution is in progress for the device range(s). Please wait...

        Polling for Establish.............................................Not Needed.

        Polling for Activate..............................................Started.

        Polling for Activate..............................................Done.

    Establish operation successfully executed for the device range(s)

    dsib2028:~ #

    • Create a new storage group with the single device in it. Set the SRP and Service Level to NONE, otherwise the creation will error because a single device cannot have two SRPs or Service Levels. Then use the Data Protection wizard to take a snapshot of the storage group.

    Figure 91.    Step 1 – LVM snapshot restore to new target

    Figure 92.    Step 1 – LVM snapshot restore to new target

    Step 2

    Link the storage group to the snapshot either through CLI or Unisphere. After linking the snapshot, it is useful to obtain the WWN of the target volume. This saves a step, so you don’t have to query the volume on the target Proxmox node. In Figure 93, the LVM device 1D6 links to 1A2 (inset) with a WWN ending in 132.

    Figure 93.    Step 2 – LVM snapshot restore to new target

    Step 3

    If you employ multipathing, add the alias for the newly linked device to the multipath.conf file on each host in the target cluster. In this example, we match the alias to the snapshot source device, rather than the new device to avoid confusion concerning the LVM.

            …

      path_grouping_policy    group_by_prio

            path_checker            tur

            failback                immediate

            fast_io_fail_tmo        5

            no_path_retry           3

            rr_min_io               1

            max_sectors_kb          1024

            dev_loss_tmo            10

        }

    }

    multipaths {

        multipath {

            wwid  360000970000120002165533030314132

            alias pmax-1D6

        }

    }

    Step 4

    Create a masking view for the linked storage group.

    Figure 94.    Step 4 – LVM snapshot restore to new target

    Rescan the target Proxmox cluster hosts and then reload multipathing. On this test cluster there are only two paths rather than four.

    root@pmax186:~# multipath -r

    root@pmax186:~# multipath -ll

    pmax-1D6 (360000970000120002165533030314132) dm-5 EMC,SYMMETRIX

    size=2.0T features='1 queue_if_no_path' hwhandler='0' wp=rw

    `-+- policy='service-time 0' prio=1 status=active

      |- 16:0:0:0 sdb 8:16 active ready running

      `- 18:0:0:0 sdc 8:32 active ready running

    Step 5

    To complete the restore, run a pvscan followed by a vgscan on each host. It should discover the existing physical volume and volume group. Note that unlike when adding a new device to hosts in a cluster, since the pv and vg exist already on the device, you will not need to reboot hosts.

    root@pmax186:~# pvscan

      PV /dev/sda3                    VG pve        lvm2 [<14.42 GiB / 8.00 MiB free]

      PV /dev/mapper/pmax-1D6-part1   VG pmax-1D6   lvm2 [<2.00 TiB / 1.63 TiB free]

      Total: 2 [2.01 TiB] / in use: 2 [2.01 TiB] / in no VG: 0 [0   ]

    root@pmax186:~# vgscan

      Found volume group "pve" using metadata type lvm2

      Found volume group "pmax-1D6" using metadata type lvm2

    Once each host sees the volume group, access the Proxmox UI and add the LVM.

    Figure 95.    Step 5 – LVM snapshot restore to new target

    Since both the physical volume and volume group already exist, all hosts in the cluster will have immediate access to the LVM.

    Figure 96.    Step 5 – LVM snapshot restore to new target

    Step 6

    Finally, copy over any VM configuration files from the vm-confs NFS share to the local host. Do not copy the same file to both hosts. You can copy them all to one host or divide them between the hosts. Here, we copy the VM with ID 100 to host pmax186.

    root@pmax186:/mnt/pve/vm-confs/snippets# cp 100.conf /etc/pve/qemu-server/

    Almost immediately after you copy the file, Proxmox will recognize the VM and make it available in the UI.

    Figure 97.    Step 6 – LVM snapshot restore to new target

    Note: Proxmox will not validate the contents of the VM configuration files. If the VM has a disk that is located on storage that is unavailable to the cluster, when you try to manipulate the VM, e.g., power on, it will error. This is particularly important if you decide to name the snapshot LVM something different than the source. Proxmox cannot automatically update the configuration file. In such circumstances, you must manually modify the VM configuration files to match your renamed LVM.

Cluster creation

  • Follow these steps to create a Proxmox cluster with the installed nodes. In this paper, there are three nodes.

    Step 1

    In the Proxmox UI of the first cluster node, navigate to Datacenter > Cluster  and click Create Cluster.

    Figure 13.    Step 1 – Create a Proxmox cluster

    Step 2

    Enter a Cluster Name. Link 0 defaults to the management network. If you have a second network, click Add for Link 1 and use the drop-down to select the IP. This provides redundancy. Proxmox supports up to eight links. The instructions for configuring a second network are in the Appendix. Click Create.

    Figure 14.    Step 2 – Create a Proxmox cluster

    Step 3

    In the same Cluster screen, click Join Information.

    Figure 15.    Step 3 – Create a Proxmox cluster

    In the pop-up dialog below, click Copy Information.

    Figure 16.    Step 3 – Create a Proxmox cluster

    Step 4

    Log in to one of the other Proxmox nodes and navigate to Datacenter > Cluster and click Join Cluster.

    Figure 17.    Step 4 – Create a Proxmox cluster

    Step 5

    Paste the copied information from Figure 16 into the Information field below. Enter the Password of the first node in the cluster and make sure the Links map properly using the drop-down menus. Click Join <cluster> to complete.

    Figure 18.    Step 5 – Create a Proxmox cluster

    As the node joins the cluster, the Task viewer will display the following authentication error. It is expected.

    Figure 19.    Step 5 – Create a Proxmox cluster

    Step 6

    Complete the addition of the other node, then log in to the Proxmox UI of any cluster node to display the cluster.

    Figure 20.    Step 6 – Create a Proxmox cluster

    Scaling

    Proxmox cluster expansion is straightforward. The process to add a node mirrors the node installation above, allowing you to scale the environment to manage increased VM and LXC container workloads.

Cross-cluster migration

  • With two Proxmox clusters, we can now perform an online cross-cluster migration of a VM. Follow this procedure below.

    Step 1

    In Datacenter Manager, navigate to Remotes in the left-hand menu and highlight the cluster (pmax-cluster) with the source VM. Under Resources in the right-hand panel, highlight the chosen VM (200) and click the Migrate icon shaped like a paper airplane.

    Figure 123.          Step 1 – Cross-cluster migration

    Step 2

    Select the Target Remote, Target Storage, and Target Network from the respective drop-down menus. If you wish to remove the source after the migration, click the Delete Source check box. Click Migrate.

    Figure 124.          Step 2 – Cross-cluster migration

    Step 3

    Use the Task viewer to monitor the migration until completion.

    Figure 125.          Step 3 – Cross-cluster migration

    Step 4

    When the migration finishes, it will display the time the VM was “down” or paused, which is expected. In this case, it was 70 ms.

    Figure 126.          Step 4 – Cross-cluster migration

    The 200 VM is now available on the other cluster, pmax-2-cluster.

    Figure 127.          Step 4 – Cross-cluster migration

Document purpose

  • This document provides configuration and deployment guidance for implementing Proxmox Virtual Environment and Proxmox Datacenter Manager with Dell PowerMax storage. It describes how to deploy a Proxmox VE cluster using shared block and file storage from PowerMax and how to configure core virtualization and storage workflows required for enterprise environments.

    Specifically, the document covers:

    • Installation and configuration of a Proxmox VE cluster, including:
    • Cluster formation, node configuration, and high availability enablement with affinity rules
    • Integration with Proxmox Datacenter Manager for centralized cluster visibility
    • Integration of Dell PowerMax storage with Proxmox, including:
    • Fibre channel block storage configuration using LVM2 (thick) and device‑mapper multipathing
    • NFS storage integration for shared access across all cluster nodes
    • Storage operations and data protection workflows, including:
    • Creation and restoration of PowerMax SnapVX snapshots
    • Reattachment and reuse of restored snapshot devices within Proxmox LVM storage pools
    • Configuration and usage of Proxmox shared‑LVM snapshots, including:
    • Snapshot creation workflows and operational behavior
    • Performance and functional considerations related to qcow2 disks and technology preview limitations

    This document demonstrates how Proxmox Virtual Environment and Dell PowerMax operate together to provide shared storage, high availability, and enterprise data protection capabilities for virtual machine and container workloads.

    Note: The contents of this document are valid for the software and hardware versions described. For information about updated configurations for newer software and hardware versions, contact your Proxmox or Dell Technologies sales representative.

File system

  • Step 1

    Navigate to embedded Unisphere (external does not support File) and the Storage > File option in the left-hand menu. Click Create under the File Systems tab.

    Figure 80.    Step 1 – Create NFS

    Step 2

    Select the type of file system. The default is General and is appropriate for Proxmox. Click Next.

    Figure 81.    Step 2 – Create NFS

    Step 3

    Select an available NAS Server. Note that the server does not require SMB for Proxmox. Click Next.

    Figure 82.    Step 3 – Create NFS

    Step 4

    In File System Details, enter a Name, Description (if desired), and Size. Click Next to the File Level Retention (FLR) screen. The default is Off and accepted. Click Next again to move to the NFS Export step.

    Figure 83.    Step 4 – Create NFS

    Step 5

    Enter a Name and Description (if desired) for the export. Toggle the button Configure the initial Export. Record this information for later use. Click Next.

    Figure 84.    Step 5 – Create NFS

    Step 6

    In the Configure Access screen, leave the default Minimum Security as System and set the Default Access to Read/Write, allow Root. Click Next.

    Figure 85.    Step 6 – Create NFS

    Step 7

    Review the Summary and click Run In The Background.

    Figure 86.    Step 7 – Create NFS

Graphical install failure

  • Sometimes when installing with the graphical interface, Proxmox will fail trying to partition the chosen device. It is unclear why this occurs, but once it does, repeating the installation will not succeed. There are two options: format or wipe the device completely with iDRAC or another management utility before retrying or restart the installer but use the Terminal UI instead. Both of these options avoid the issue.

Home > Storage > PowerMax and VMAX > White Papers > Implementing Proxmox 9 on Dell PowerMax > HA Affinity Rules

HA Affinity Rules

  • Proxmox 9 utilizes HA Affinity Rules, Resource and Node, to ensure you can fence VMs from each other, either by restricting VMs to certain hosts or preventing particular VMs from running on the same host. You configure these most easily in the UI as follows.

    Figure 48.    HA Affinity Rules

    VM HA

    You can only apply Affinity Rules to VMs that are marked as HA. To enable HA, navigate to the VM in the left-hand panel in the Proxmox UI and select Manage HA from the right-hand More menu. Note the HA State is currently none.

    Figure 49.    Manage HA for a VM

    The Request State will default to started, so simply click Add to enable HA.

    Figure 50.    Enable HA for a VM

    Now, we will walk through the creation of an HA Node and Resource Affinity Rule. For these examples, we use two Oracle RAC VMs, 102 and 103, which we want to run on different nodes to provide the best availability and resource distribution. The two rule methods produce the same result, albeit each in their own way.

    HA Node Affinity rule

    To create a new HA Node Affinity rule for a VM, follow these steps.

    Step 1

    In Figure 48, click Add in the top HA Node Affinity Rules panel.

    Step 2

    Using the HA Resources drop-down, highlight the VMs you want as part of the node rule. We chose VM 102, which is Oracle RAC node 1.

    Figure 51.    Step 2 – HA Node Affinity rule

    Step 3

    Decide on which hosts the VM can run. You can choose one or more and then set an optional Priority. For this VM, we let it run on any node but set a priority for each. The Strict checkbox serves no purpose here since we allow the VM to run on any node. If we did not want the VM to run on pmax176, for example, we would uncheck the box and turn on Strict. This would prevent the VM from running on pmax176 no matter what the state is of pmax172 and pmax174. Click Add to complete.

    Figure 52.    Step 3 – HA Node Affinity rule

    Now, configure Oracle RAC node 2 but reverse the Priority. Note that pmax174 will be priority 2 for both. Click Add.

    Figure 53.    Step 3 – HA Node Affinity rule

    Review the new rules in the following panel.

    Figure 54.    HA Node Affinity rules

    HA Resource Affinity rule

    To create a new HA Resource Affinity rule for VMs, follow these steps.

    Step 1

    In Figure 48, click Add in the bottom HA Resource Affinity Rules panel.

    Step 2

    Using the HA Resources drop-down, select the VMs you want as part of the resource rule. You must select a minimum of two. Here, we select both Oracle RAC nodes. Then under Affinity, use the drop-down to select Keep Separate. This ensures that the VMs will not run on the same host. Click Add.

    Figure 55.    Step 2 – HA Resource Affinity rule

    Review the new rule in Figure 56. This rule is a negative Affinity rule. Had we set the Affinity to Keep Together, it would be a positive Affinity rule.

    Figure 56.    HA Resource Affinity rule

    Be aware that if the Node and Resource rules perform the same function as here, you cannot enable both at the same time. Any attempt to do so will result in an error, as shown here.

    Figure 57.    Multiple rules blocked

    In addition, when using Affinity Rules, Proxmox will prevent any VM migration that violates the rules. For example, if VM 102 is running on pmax176 and VM 103 is running on pmax172 and you try to migrate VM 102 to pmax172, you will receive the following error:

    Figure 58.    Migration blocked due to Affinity Rule

    Affinity Rules can be an effective way to ensure distribution particularly for clustered applications like Oracle RAC.

Leveraging PowerMax snapshots for VM reuse and recovery

  • SnapVX is a local replication solution that creates point-in-time copies, or snapshots, of PowerMax devices. SnapVX creates snapshots by storing changed tracks (deltas) directly in the SRP of the source volume. With SnapVX, you do not need to specify a target volume and source/target pairs when you create a snapshot. If the application ever needs to use the point-in-time data, you can create links from the snapshot to one or more target volumes. If there are multiple snapshots and the application needs to find a particular point-in-time copy for host access, you can link and relink until the correct snapshot is located. Snapshots are crash-consistent copies of the data.

    Note: There is no relationship between SnapVX and the Proxmox snapshot technology preview in the section, LVM chain snapshots (technology preview). If you use SnapVX for your snapshot business requirements, it is best to not enable the technology preview. It adds no value in this design and can introduce unnecessary performance overhead.

    The next sections show how customers can use SnapVX in a Proxmox environment for two common workflows: creating reusable copies of virtual machines and restoring existing virtual machines to an earlier point in time. These workflows build on the earlier NFS configuration, which stores Proxmox virtual machine configuration files on shared storage and supports safe snapshot-based operations across the environment.

    For these sections, keep these definitions in mind:

    • Reuse refers to attaching a SnapVX copy as a new LVM to create an additional virtual machine.
    • Restore refers to rolling back an existing LVM and its associated virtual machine to a previous point in time.

Management Interfaces

  • Proxmox VE Web Interface

    Proxmox VE includes a native web interface on every node and cluster. Administrators use this interface to manage nodes, virtual machines, containers, storage, networking, updates, and high availability within that specific Proxmox VE environment. In a cluster, an administrator can log in to any node and manage the cluster from that node’s interface.

    Access the UI through the following URL: https://<FQDN>:8006. An example follows.

    Figure 2.   Proxmox VE native web interface for single-cluster management

    Proxmox Datacenter Manager Interface

    Proxmox Datacenter Manager provides a separate centralized interface for environments that contain multiple Proxmox VE clusters or other Proxmox remotes. It connects to managed clusters through authenticated APIs, aggregates inventory and operational state, and lets administrators perform supported management tasks across clusters without replacing each cluster’s local control plane.

    Access the UI through the following URL: https://<FQDN>:8443. An example follows.

    Figure 3.   Proxmox Datacenter Manager interface for centralized multi-cluster management

    Interface Scope

    Use the Proxmox VE interface when you want to operate a single cluster directly. Use Datacenter Manager when you want a unified view across multiple clusters, centralized dashboards, and operations such as cross-cluster migration.

Multipathing

  • Begin by installing two additional packages on each host: lsscsi and multipath-tools. The lsscsi binary will help identify the WWN of the PowerMax devices.

    The following is a sample multipath.conf file for PowerMax FC on Proxmox. This file uses find_multipaths set to yes rather than the Proxmox recommendation of strict. When the setting is strict, you must add new devices to /etc/multipath/wwids. When set to yes, multipath will find any presented devices from PowerMax. The bold multipath aliases at the bottom of the file are examples. They are only needed if you wish to alias the device rather than use the default naming, e.g., /dev/mapper/mpathx.

    multipath.conf

    defaults {

        polling_interval    5

        checker_timeout     15

        user_friendly_names no

        find_multipaths     yes

    }

    blacklist {

        devnode ^hd[a-z][0-9]*$

        devnode ^sda$

    }

    devices {

        device {

            vendor                  EMC

            product                 SYMMETRIX

            detect_prio             yes

            path_selector           “service-time 0”

            path_grouping_policy    group_by_prio

            path_checker            tur

            failback                immediate

            fast_io_fail_tmo        5

            no_path_retry           3

            rr_min_io               1

            max_sectors_kb          1024

            dev_loss_tmo            10

        }

    }

    multipaths {

        multipath {

            wwid  360000970000120002165533030314436

            alias pmax-1D6

        }

        multipath {

            wwid  360000970000120002165533030314536

            alias pmax-1E6

        }

        multipath {

            wwid  360000970000120002165533030314538

            alias pmax-1E8

        }

    }

    When making changes to the multipath.conf, reload it by running multipath -r. Running this command is also necessary after adding new devices to the nodes if you add aliases to the configuration file.

    New device multipathing

    To add a new alias to the multipath.conf file, you must first determine the WWN. If you have access to Unisphere, you can find it there, but if you need to discover the WWN from the Proxmox host, use the lsscsi utility.

    In this example, we provision 200 GB to the Proxmox cluster.

    Step 1

    Rescan each Proxmox node to discover the new volume. The script, rescan-scsi-bus.sh, is an effective tool for this. The following is an example scan, condensed for space, which shows that there are four new devices. In fact, there are four paths for the same device.

    root@pmax172:/# rescan-scsi-bus.sh

    Scanning SCSI subsystem for new devices

    Scanning host 0 for  SCSI target IDs 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7, all LUNs

     Scanning for device 0 2 0 0 ...

    Scanning host 1 for  SCSI target IDs 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7, all LUNs

    Scanning host 2 for  SCSI target IDs 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7, all LUNs

    Scanning host 3 for  SCSI target IDs 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7, all LUNs

    Scanning host 18 for  all SCSI target IDs, all LUNs

     Scanning for device 18 0 0 0 ...

    NEW:  Host: scsi18 Channel: 00 Id: 00 Lun: 04

          Vendor: EMC      Model: SYMMETRIX        Rev: 6079

          Type:   Direct-Access                    ANSI SCSI revision: 05

     Scanning for device 18 0 1 0 ...

    NEW:  Host: scsi18 Channel: 00 Id: 01 Lun: 04

          Vendor: EMC      Model: SYMMETRIX        Rev: 6079

          Type:   Direct-Access                    ANSI SCSI revision: 05

    Scanning host 19 for  all SCSI target IDs, all LUNs

    NEW:  Host: scsi19 Channel: 00 Id: 01 Lun: 04

          Vendor: EMC      Model: SYMMETRIX        Rev: 6079

          Type:   Direct-Access                    ANSI SCSI revision: 05

     Scanning for device 19 0 0 0 ...

    Scanning for device 19 0 0 4 ...

    NEW:  Host: scsi19 Channel: 00 Id: 00 Lun: 04

          Vendor: EMC      Model: SYMMETRIX        Rev: 6079

          Type:   Direct-Access                    ANSI SCSI revision: 05

    4 new or changed device(s) found.

            [18:0:0:4]

            [18:0:1:4]

            [19:0:1:4]

            [19:0:0:4]

    0 remapped or resized device(s) found.

    0 device(s) removed.

    Step 2

    Run the lsscsi command with the –scsi_id switch to see the device WWNs. They are listed by host and channel which you can cross-reference with step 1 (list condensed below). Comparing the two, we see four added items of WWN  360000970000120002165533030314542. If you do not have the values from the rescan, use fdisk -l to determine the new /dev/sdx devices and use those for comparison.

    root@pmax172:/# lsscsi --scsi_id

    [18:0:1:3] disk    EMC  SYMMETRIX 6079  /dev/sdp 360000970000120002165533030314539

    [18:0:0:4] disk    EMC  SYMMETRIX 6079  /dev/sds 360000970000120002165533030314542

    [18:0:1:4] disk    EMC  SYMMETRIX 6079  /dev/sdt 360000970000120002165533030314542

    [19:0:0:0] disk    EMC  SYMMETRIX 6079  /dev/sdg 360000970000120002165533030314436

    [19:0:0:1] disk    EMC  SYMMETRIX 6079  /dev/sdh 360000970000120002165533030314536

    [19:0:0:2] disk    EMC  SYMMETRIX 6079  /dev/sdn 360000970000120002165533030314538

    [19:0:0:3] disk    EMC  SYMMETRIX 6079  /dev/sdr 360000970000120002165533030314539

    [19:0:0:4] disk    EMC  SYMMETRIX 6079  /dev/sdv 360000970000120002165533030314542

    [19:0:1:4] disk    EMC  SYMMETRIX 6079  /dev/sdu 360000970000120002165533030314542

    Step 3

    Update the /etc/multipath.conf file on each Proxmox host with a new alias.

       multipath {

            wwid  360000970000120002165533030314542

            alias pmax-1EB

        }

    Then run multipath -r and multipath -ll on each host to see the new device.

    root@pmax172:/# multipath -r

    root@pmax172:/# multipath -ll

    pmax-1EB (360000970000120002165533030314542) dm-13 EMC,SYMMETRIX

    size=200G features='1 queue_if_no_path' hwhandler='0' wp=rw

    `-+- policy='service-time 0' prio=1 status=active

      |- 18:0:0:4 sds 65:32 active ready running

      |- 18:0:1:4 sdt 65:48 active ready running

      |- 19:0:0:4 sdv 65:80 active ready running

      `- 19:0:1:4 sdu 65:64 active ready running

    The device is now ready for use by Proxmox.

    Proxmox LVM

    Using the previous device, create a new LVM in Proxmox.

    Step 1

    Create a new partition on the device and check it. Be sure to use the multipath device name. If you use one of the /dev/sdx names, it will cause issues with multipathing.

    root@pmax172:/# sgdisk -N 1 /dev/mapper/pmax-1EB

    Creating new GPT entries in memory.

    Warning: The kernel is still using the old partition table.

    The new table will be used at the next reboot or after you

    run partprobe(8) or kpartx(8)

    The operation has completed successfully.

    root@pmax172:/# fdisk -l |grep pmax-1EB

    Partition 1 does not start on physical sector boundary.

    Disk /dev/mapper/pmax-1EB: 200 GiB, 214749020160 bytes, 419431680 sectors

    /dev/mapper/pmax-1EB-part1  2048 419431646 419429599  200G Linux filesystem

    Step 2

    Create a new physical volume. Proxmox recommends a metadata size of 250k.

    root@pmax172:/# pvcreate --metadatasize 250k -y -ff /dev/mapper/pmax-1EB-part1

      Physical volume "/dev/mapper/pmax-1EB-part1" successfully created.

    Step 3

    Create the volume group. Name it as you desire. Here we maintain the volume name.

    root@pmax172:/# vgcreate pmax-1EB /dev/mapper/pmax-1EB-part1

      Volume group "pmax-1EB" successfully created.

    Step 4

    Confirm the physical volume (pv) and volume group (vg). Run these commands on the same Proxmox host as the previous steps. The other hosts in the cluster will not see these until after you reboot them.

    root@pmax172:/# pvscan

      PV /dev/mapper/pmax-1EB-part1        VG pmax-1EB        lvm2 [<200.00 GiB / <200.00 GiB free]

    root@pmax172:/# vgscan

      Found volume group "pmax-1EB" using metadata type lvm2

    Open the Proxmox UI and navigate to Datacenter (<your cluster>) in the left-hand side and then Storage in the right-hand side. Click the Add drop-down button and select LVM.

    Figure 25.    Step 4 – Proxmox LVM

    Step 5

    Enter in an ID (name) and use the Volume group drop-down to select the vg, in this case pmax-1EB. Check the box for Shared and, if desired, Wipe Removed Volumes. If you want to test the snapshot technology preview, check Allow Snapshots as Volume-Chain. For more details, see LVM chain snapshots (technology preview). Click Add.

    Figure 26.    Step 5 – Proxmox LVM

    After creation, the LVM is available on the initial node—here pmax172—but the other nodes will show a question mark until you reboot the hosts. To facilitate the reboots, use the bulk migrate capabilities to move VMs to another host with shared storage if necessary.

    Figure 27.    Step 5 – Proxmox LVM

Networking

  • MTU

    If you plan on using a larger MTU than 1500, e.g., 9000, you can modify the NICs either using the Linux CLI or the Proxmox UI. Note that you must increase the physical NIC MTU before you can increase the bridge or VLAN associated with that NIC.

    Management VLAN

    If your management interface requires a VLAN, you must modify the network in the console after the installation completes. The following example is from the installation in this paper where we modify the /etc/network/interfaces file directly. NIC4 has the management interface, and we reconfigure it to use VLAN 100. We then run ifreload -a. Note the MTU is adjusted to 9000 at the same time.

    auto lo

    iface lo inet loopback

    auto nic4

    iface nic4 inet manual

            mtu 9000

    iface nic0 inet manual

    iface nic1 inet manual

    iface nic2 inet manual

    iface nic3 inet manual

    auto nic5

    iface nic5 inet manual

            mtu 9000

    auto vmbr0

    iface vmbr0 inet static

            bridge-ports nic4

            bridge-stp off

            bridge-fd 0

            bridge-vlan-aware yes

            bridge-vids 2-4094

       mtu 9000

    auto vmbr0.100

    iface vmbr0.100 inet static

            address 172.20.100.176/24

            gateway 172.20.100.44

      mtu 9000

    Be aware that if you use this interface for the VM network, it will not inherit the VLAN. You must supply that on the network interface of the VM.

    Additional management network

    Proxmox recommends cluster network redundancy to ensure connectivity. In this environment, we create a second network on a different NIC and VLAN for this purpose. The steps are as follows.

    Step 1

    Highlight the Proxmox node in the left-hand panel and then System > Network. Select Create > Linux Bridge. 

    Figure 130.          Step 1 – Additional management network

    Step 2

    The Name defaults to the next vmbr name, here vmbr1. Check the VLAN aware box, and in Bridge ports, type in the physical NIC. Enter an MTU setting and click Create. Note that your MTU cannot be higher than the bridge port NIC.

    Figure 131.          Step 2 – Additional management network

    Step 3

    Return to Figure 130 and follow the same steps but now select Linux VLAN. Type in a Name of your choice (it will default to vlan0) and the IP address. If you use the Name syntax below, Proxmox will fill in the Vlan raw device and VLAN Tag; otherwise, you must fill them in manually. Enter in an MTU and click Create.

    Figure 132.          Step 3 – Additional management network

    Step 4

    In the Network screen, click Apply Configuration.

    Figure 133.          Step 4 – Additional management network

    You can view the results of this example in Figure 134.

    Figure 134.          Step 4 – Additional management network

    When you complete the section Cluster creation, use this second network for redundancy.

Overview

  • This paper explains how to deploy and operate Proxmox Virtual Environment 9 with Dell PowerMax as shared enterprise storage. This paper will give administrators a practical implementation model for building a three-node Proxmox cluster that uses PowerMax Fibre Channel block storage for shared LVM and PowerMax NFS for file-based services. The paper also shows how to connect Proxmox Datacenter Manager for centralized visibility across clusters and for cross-cluster operations.

    The document focuses on the core workflows that matter in production: cluster installation, node joining, shared storage provisioning, multipathing, LVM creation, VM and container deployment, and high-availability configuration. It also maps those workflows to PowerMax capabilities such as service levels, masking views, SnapVX snapshots, and file services. That combination gives infrastructure teams a clear path to deliver shared storage, workload mobility, and operational consistency without adopting a hyperconverged design.

    A major theme of the paper is storage behavior and data protection. It distinguishes between Proxmox shared-LVM snapshot chains and native PowerMax SnapVX snapshots, and it shows where each approach fits. The paper positions SnapVX as the stronger option for enterprise recovery and VM reuse workflows because it supports point-in-time copies and restores at the array layer while avoiding the performance tradeoffs that Proxmox volume-chain snapshots can introduce.

    The paper also highlights the operational model around the platform. It documents how teams can provision new storage, present it across all hosts, monitor the environment with external telemetry platforms such as InfluxDB and Grafana, and recover or clone workloads by combining shared storage with Proxmox configuration management. It also explains how Datacenter Manager extends that model beyond a single cluster by adding centralized inventory and cross-cluster migration.

    Overall, the paper serves as an implementation and operations guide for storage, virtualization, and system administrators who want to pair Proxmox with Dell PowerMax in a production-oriented design. It shows how the architecture works, what components it requires, and how administrators can run key lifecycle tasks across deployment, protection, recovery, and growth.

PowerMax

  • The PowerMax family represents the flagship products of the Dell Technologies enterprise storage business. It is a multi-node, active/active scale-out architecture using industry standard end-to-end NVMe components. The platform features inline, global deduplication and compression, providing customers with high storage efficiency even as the system scales. The PowerMax family also provides what many consider to be the gold standard in data services, proven high availability and resiliency, and advanced security that adheres to stringent government regulations and corporate compliance requirements such as FIPS 140-2 and FIPS 140-3. A core strength of the PowerMax family is its ability to consolidate workloads. One can use a single PowerMax system to consolidate from one-to-many types of workloads and both block and file storage services.

    PowerMax systems are modular, enabling them to expand to meet the future needs of the customer. The PowerMax family of arrays has four models:

    • PowerMax 2500 with a maximum capacity of 8 PBe (Petabytes effective)
    • PowerMax 2000 with a maximum capacity of 1.2 PBe
    • PowerMax 8500 with a maximum capacity of 18 PBe
    • PowerMax 8000 with a maximum capacity of 4.5 PBe

    Dell Technologies configures the PowerMax at the factory with a single Storage Resource Pool, or SRP, which is comprised of the physical disks in the array managed as data pools. The array uses this collection of data pools for capacity and performance management. All host devices are part of an SRP.

    PowerMax for Open Systems provides support for the following protocols:

    • Fiber-Channel (FC) and NVMe over FC (NVMe/FC) with speeds of 16/32/64/128 G.
    • SRDF over FC
    • iSCSI and NVMe over TCP (NVMe/TCP) with speed of 10/25/100 Gb/E
    • SRDF over IP

    PowerMaxOS operating system

    PowerMaxOS is the advanced operating system that powers Dell PowerMax storage arrays, delivering a purpose-driven, performance-optimized platform designed for mission-critical enterprise workloads. It is a modern architecture that is modular, container-based, and tightly integrated with end-to-end NVMe hardware to offer ultra-low latency, high throughput, and automated efficiency.

    Built with intelligent machine learning, PowerMaxOS dynamically analyzes I/O patterns to optimize data placement and resource usage in real time. It supports inline compression and de-duplication, ensuring space efficiency. With native encryption, secure snapshots, and multi-tenancy features, PowerMaxOS also ensures strong data protection and isolation.

    PowerMax replication

    PowerMax local replication includes TimeFinder SnapVX (snapshots) and TimeFinder/Clone (clones), while PowerMax remote replication includes the SRDF product line. TimeFinder provides point-in-time local replication and data protection, and SRDF provides continuous remote replication, high availability, and disaster recovery.

    You can initiate or restore PowerMax snapshots or clones on SRDF target devices. One benefit of this integration is that it allows the creation of remote copies of the source application without interrupting remote replication. If the source application data is corrupted, the remote snapshot (or clone) and SRDF can restore the data in parallel to the source volumes. SRDF sends only changed data during normal operation and utilizes write folding to reduce the network impact.

PowerMax data allocation

  • Whether or not the LVM snapshot feature is in use, PowerMax will only allocate new storage extents for unique data. For example, we create a new VM with a 34 GB device and install an operating system. This results in allocating 3 GB.

    [root@pmax-dedup ~]# df

    Filesystem           1K-blocks    Used Available Use% Mounted on

    devtmpfs                  4096       0      4096   0% /dev

    tmpfs                  1871256       0   1871256   0% /dev/shm

    tmpfs                   748504    8716    739788   2% /run

    /dev/mapper/rlm-root  29077504 2728656  26348848  10% /

    /dev/sda1               983040  361816    621224  37% /boot

    tmpfs                   374248       0    374248   0% /run/user/0

    Proxmox reports 34 GB in use on the LVM because of thick provisioning.

    Figure 76.    Proxmox storage allocation of the VM

    When we check the device on the array, it reports only 3 GB in use (1%) or the actual allocation on the operating system.

    Figure 77.    Unisphere for PowerMax storage allocation of the VM

    If we now create a snapshot on the VM, the LVM reports another 34 GB allocation for a total of 68 GB.

    Figure 78.    Proxmox storage allocation of the VM with a snapshot

    When we return to Unisphere, the size is the same because the snapshot creation did not actually allocate extents. Creating a snapshot in Proxmox renames the original VM volume and instantiates a new logical volume, which causes Proxmox to account for another full‑size disk. On PowerMax, however, no new extents are allocated until the snapshot diverges from the original data.

    Figure 79.    Unisphere for PowerMax storage allocation of the VM

    PowerMax data reduction

    When the LVM volume containing Proxmox VM disks resides in a PowerMax storage group with data reduction enabled, the array guarantees that identical blocks are never stored more than once, even when Proxmox reports additional space consumption due to thick‑provisioned LVM snapshots. Because PowerMax deduplication and compression operate at the array level, any unchanged blocks shared between the active VM disk and its snapshots remain single‑instanced. As a result, the physical footprint on the array grows only with new or modified data, ensuring the effective space consumption of a VM with snapshots closely tracks real data change rather than the logical size reported by Proxmox.

Prerequisites

  • You should meet the following prerequisites before implementing Proxmox with PowerMax. These are the minimum server requirements for a production deployment of Proxmox for three nodes. Note that while Proxmox does not mandate minimums, using lower values will render the system performance unacceptable for practical use.

    • Three Dell servers with a 64‑bit x86 (Intel 64 / AMD64) architecture. To achieve live migration of VMs without modification, the servers should be identical.
    • Minimum two cores.
    • Two GB RAM for the server, more for the VMs.
    • One, 1 (one) GbE NIC. Proxmox recommends two for redundancy. If using IP networking for storage, e.g., NFS as in this solution, a 10 GbE NIC is preferable.
    • Two 2-Port 32Gb Fibre Channel Adapter.

    The storage requirements for Proxmox are as follows:

    • An installed PowerMax 2500 or 8500 array.
    • At least four (4) front-end ports zoned to each Proxmox server.

    Miscellaneous requirements:

    • Port trunking for VLAN support.
    • A bastion server to access the private network.
    • A DNS and NTP server.
    • Proxmox VE 9.1.x and Proxmox Datacenter Manager 1.0.1 ISOs.

    You can find the Proxmox hardware requirements here.

Proxmox Datacenter Manager

  • Proxmox Datacenter Manager provides centralized visibility and management across one or more Proxmox VE clusters. It extends the Proxmox management model by aggregating cluster inventories and operational state into a unified management plane while allowing each cluster to retain its own control and execution services.

    Datacenter Manager does not replace the Proxmox VE cluster control plane. Instead, it connects to managed clusters through authenticated APIs to collect state, surface configuration, and coordinate administrative workflows. Each Proxmox VE cluster continues to manage workload execution, high availability, and storage access independently.

    Core Functions

    The core functions of the Proxmox Datacenter Manager are:

    • Cluster Inventory and Visibility: Datacenter Manager maintains a centralized inventory of registered Proxmox VE clusters, nodes, virtual machines, storage pools, and network resources, presenting their health, status, and utilization.
    • Operational Coordination: Administrators use Datacenter Manager to perform cross cluster operational tasks, monitor workload placement, and maintain consistent management practices without logging into individual clusters.
    • Access and Authentication Integration: Centralized authentication and role mapping provide controlled access to clusters and resources while preserving native Proxmox permission models.

    Management Plane Components

    The management plane componentes of the Proxmox Datacenter Manager are:

    • Datacenter Manager Service: Provides the web interface and API endpoints for centralized management, inventory aggregation, and administrative control.
    • Managed Proxmox VE Clusters: Independent Proxmox VE clusters register with Datacenter Manager and expose state and configuration for centralized visibility without relinquishing local control.

  • After creating the file system, create the Proxmox NFS storage.

    Step 1

    Open the UI and navigate to Datacenter (<your cluster>) in the left-hand side and then Storage in the right-hand menu. Click the Add drop-down button and select NFS.

    Figure 87.    Step 1 – Create Proxmox NFS

    Step 2

    In the dialog box, type in an ID (name), then the Server IP of the PowerMax NFS server. Next to the Export field, click the down arrow and the available file systems will appear. The Content will default to Disk image. If you want to permit additional types, use the drop-down to select those. Click Add to complete the wizard.

    Figure 88.    Step 2 – Create Proxmox NFS

    Unlike an LVM, the Proxmox NFS is available to all nodes immediately without requiring a reboot since it is IP-based, not FC.

    Figure 89.    Proxmox NFS across all nodes in a cluster

Proxmox VE

  • Proxmox Virtual Environment (VE) is an open-source virtualization platform designed for running and managing virtual machines and Linux containers on standard x86 64 servers. It builds on the Linux Kernel based Virtual Machine (KVM) hypervisor and Linux Containers (LXC), providing an integrated stack for compute virtualization, clustering, storage integration, and high availability within a single platform.

    A Proxmox VE cluster consists of one or more nodes running a general-purpose Linux operating system with the Proxmox kernel, virtualization services, and cluster management components. Each node hosts virtual machines and containers directly on the hypervisor without an intermediate abstraction layer. Administrators manage resources through a unified web interface, command line tools, and REST APIs.

    Proxmox VE implements clustering through a distributed configuration database and quorum-based coordination services. Cluster membership enables shared configuration, coordinated scheduling, and high availability across nodes while keeping virtual machine definitions, storage metadata, and overall cluster state consistent across all members.

    The hypervisor runs virtual machines on KVM and manages them directly within the platform. Virtual disks connect through cluster-level storage backends, which lets administrators present shared access to external block or file storage across nodes. Proxmox natively supports both raw and qcow2 disk formats, and when shared storage is available, it supports live migration between nodes without requiring a hyperconverged storage model.

    Cluster Architecture

    A Proxmox VE cluster is composed of one or more nodes that collectively provide virtualization, cluster coordination, and workload execution services.

    • Cluster and Control Services: Proxmox nodes participate in a clustered control plane that maintains configuration state, node membership, and quorum. These services coordinate cluster operations such as VM scheduling, migration, and high availability decisions while ensuring consistent visibility across nodes.
    • Virtualization and Workload Services: Each node runs KVM and LXC workloads locally. VM placement and migration are administrator-driven, while CPU and memory scheduling, isolation, and limits are enforced by the Linux kernel on each host. Proxmox provides HA and tooling but does not perform automatic cluster-wide workload scheduling or rebalancing.
    • Storage Integration: Proxmox integrates with shared block and file storage systems to provide persistent VM disks across the cluster. Storage pools abstract underlying storage devices and expose them to virtual machines in a consistent manner. This design enables live migration, HA restart, and centralized storage management without embedding storage services into the hypervisor layer.
    • Networking Services: Proxmox configures node level networking to support VM to VM communication, external connectivity, and cluster interconnect traffic. Software defined bridges and interfaces provide Layer 2 and Layer 3 connectivity while allowing administrators to integrate with existing physical networks.

    Figure 1 illustrates a representative Proxmox VE cluster deployment, showing the relationship between cluster coordination services, virtualization components, shared storage, and networking.

    Figure 1.   Proxmox architecture

    Dell PowerMax storage

    In a Proxmox VE cluster, Dell PowerMax provides shared persistent storage for virtual machines and containers. Unlike a local disk on a single node, the shared array storage keeps data available during node maintenance, failover, and workload migration. It also supports key Proxmox capabilities such as live migration, high availability, centralized storage management, and consistent performance across the cluster. These capabilities matter most for stateful workloads such as databases, application servers, and other enterprise services that need reliable access to their data at all times.

    Dell PowerMax also lets you align storage performance with workload requirements. You can present different classes of storage to Proxmox based on the performance and service characteristics you need, then assign the right storage (e.g., LVM) to each VM or container. That approach helps you place business-critical workloads on higher-performance storage while keeping fewer demanding workloads on lower-cost tiers.

    Service levels

    A service level is a property of a storage group, a provisioning object on Dell PowerMax. The service level defines the maximum and minimum response times for I/O operations that involve the storage group. The minimum response time (known as the floor) defines the shortest time that each I/O operation on the storage group takes to complete. The maximum response time (known as the ceiling) defines the longest acceptable time for any I/O operation on the storage group. PowerMax uses the floor and ceiling values to monitor whether each storage group complies with its quality-of-service criteria.

    The storage administrator can use the service levels to help ensure that lower-priority applications do not impede storage groups associated with high-priority applications. The six service levels on the PowerMax are as follows, beginning with the highest priority and shown in Figure 5:

    • Diamond
    • Platinum
    • Gold
    • Silver
    • Bronze
    • Optimized

    Figure 5.   PowerMax service levels

    Under normal operating conditions, PowerMax ensures that the performance is commensurate with the chosen service level’s compliance range. If, however, there is contention, PowerMax will prioritize higher service levels by limiting performance of the lower service levels. Therefore, it is essential to select the storage class best suited for the performance needs of the VM disk or LXC container.

Recreating a virtual machine on the source cluster from a SnapVX snapshot

  • This section will cover importing an SnapVX snapshot of the LVM to the same source cluster. The Linux utility vgimportclone provides the ability to import the LVM when there is a duplicate as in this example. We provide less detail as many of the steps are the same as the previous procedure.

    For this process, it is unnecessary to copy the VM configuration files into a temporary location when using the same source hosts since the files are present. Note, however, we will have to create new VM configuration files if we wish to use the VM disks on the snapshotted LVM.

    Step 1

    Take a SnapVX snapshot of the storage group containing the LVM device. The source device in this example is 1E6, or volume group pmax-1E6.

    root@pmax172:/etc# vgs

      VG       #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize    VFree

      pmax-1D6   1  12   0 wz--n-   <2.00t    1.63t

      pmax-1E6   1   1   0 wz--n- <500.00g <468.00g

      pve        1   3   0 wz--n-  277.87g   16.00g

    Step 2

    Link the storage group to the snapshot either through CLI or Unisphere. After linking the snapshot, it is useful to obtain the WWN of the target volume. This saves a step, so you do not have to query the volume on the target Proxmox node. In this example, the WWN is 60000970000120002165533030314538.

    Step 3

    If you employ multipathing, add the alias for the newly linked device to the multipath.conf file on each host in the target cluster. When restoring to the source cluster you must use a different alias for the snapshot. In this example, we match the alias to the snapshot device rather than the new device to avoid confusion concerning the LVM. We use pmax-1E6-copy.

            …

    multipaths {

        multipath {

            wwid  360000970000120002165533030314536

            alias pmax-1E6

        }

        multipath {

            wwid  360000970000120002165533030314538

            alias pmax-1E6-copy

        }

    }

    Step 4

    Create a masking view for the linked storage group, then rescan the target Proxmox cluster hosts and reload multipathing. The new alias pmax-1E6-copy is available.

    root@pmax172:/etc# multipath -r

    root@pmax172:/etc# multipath -ll

    …

    pmax-1E6 (360000970000120002165533030314536) dm-6 EMC,SYMMETRIX

    size=500G features='1 queue_if_no_path' hwhandler='0' wp=rw

    `-+- policy='service-time 0' prio=1 status=active

      |- 18:0:0:1 sdd 8:48  active ready running

      |- 18:0:1:1 sdf 8:80  active ready running

      |- 19:0:0:1 sdh 8:112 active ready running

      `- 19:0:1:1 sdj 8:144 active ready running

    pmax-1E6-copy (360000970000120002165533030314538) dm-9 EMC,SYMMETRIX

    size=500G features='1 queue_if_no_path' hwhandler='0' wp=rw

    `-+- policy='service-time 0' prio=1 status=active

      |- 18:0:0:2 sdk 8:160 active ready running

      |- 18:0:1:2 sdl 8:176 active ready running

      |- 19:0:0:2 sdn 8:208 active ready running

      `- 19:0:1:2 sdm 8:192 active ready running

    Step 5

    To complete the restore, you must run vgimportclone to rename the copy. If you wish to double-check the device, start by running pvscan. You should see this WARNING which indicates the host found a duplicate:

    root@pmax172:/# pvscan

      WARNING: Not using device /dev/mapper/pmax-1E6-copy-part1 for PV WU9ibh-kFxK-ZFDa-7m2G-V9Vy-PcOA-RZ1iLQ.

      WARNING: PV WU9ibh-kFxK-ZFDa-7m2G-V9Vy-PcOA-RZ1iLQ prefers device /dev/mapper/pmax-1E6-part1 because device name matches previous.

      PV /dev/mapper/pmax-1E6-part1   VG pmax-1E6   lvm2 [<500.00 GiB / <468.00 GiB free]

      PV /dev/sda3                    VG pve        lvm2 [277.87 GiB / 16.00 GiB free]

      PV /dev/mapper/pmax-1D6-part1   VG pmax-1D6   lvm2 [<2.00 TiB / 1.63 TiB free]

      Total: 3 [<2.76 TiB] / in use: 3 [<2.76 TiB] / in no VG: 0 [0   ]

    root@pmax172:/#

    After confirming with pvscan, run vgimportclone and specify a desired name for the volume group. This can be whatever you wish, though we keep it the same as the volume for consistency.

    root@pmax172:/# vgimportclone --basevgname pmax-1E6-copy /dev/mapper/pmax-1E6-copy-part1

    root@pmax172:/# vgs

      VG            #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize    VFree

      pmax-1D6        1  12   0 wz--n-   <2.00t    1.63t

      pmax-1E6        1   1   0 wz--n- <500.00g <468.00g

      pmax-1E6-copy   1   1   0 wz--n- <500.00g <468.00g

      pve             1   3   0 wz--n-  277.87g   16.00g

    Now activate the volume group. First, check the attributes. An active volume group has an ‘a’ in the attributes while a dash means inactive.

    root@pmax172:/# lvs pmax-1E6-copy

      LV            VG            Attr       LSize  Pool Origin Data%  Meta%  Move Log Cpy%Sync Convert

      vm-105-disk-0 pmax-1E6-copy -wi------- 32.00g

    root@pmax172:/# vgchange -ay pmax-1E6-copy

      1 logical volume(s) in volume group "pmax-1E6-copy" now active

    root@pmax172:/# lvs pmax-1E6-copy

      LV            VG            Attr       LSize  Pool Origin Data%  Meta%  Move Log Cpy%Sync Convert

      vm-105-disk-0 pmax-1E6-copy -wi-a----- 32.00g

    Note that as long as the other nodes in the cluster see the device, no further action is necessary.

    Step 6

    In the Proxmox UI, create a new LVM referencing the copied volume group.

    Figure 98.    Step 6 – LVM snapshot restore to source cluster

    The other nodes will automatically pick up the new LVM below.

    Figure 99.    Step 6 – LVM snapshot restore to source cluster

    Step 7

    In this copied LVM, there is a single VM disk for VM 105 (pmax75.prox.com). If you wish to make this copied VM available, you must create a new VM configuration file. It is easiest to copy the existing file to a new name that is not currently in use. Do this on the node that owns the current VM.

    root@pmax174:/etc/pve/qemu-server# cp 105.conf 106.conf

    Use an editor open the file and modify the name and any disks so they reference the copied LVM:

    name: pmax75.prox.com

     to

    name: pmax76.prox.com

    scsi0: pmax-1E6:vm-105-disk-0,discard=on,iothread=1,size=32G

     to

    scsi0: pmax-1E6-copy:vm-105-disk-0,discard=on,iothread=1,size=32G

    Save the file. Proxmox will immediately display the new VM here.

    Figure 100.          Step 7 – LVM snapshot restore to source cluster

    Confirm the VM can power on. Note that you will still need to change the hostname as well as the IP if using static.

    Figure 101.          Step 7 – LVM snapshot restore to source cluster

Restoring a virtual machine from a SnapVX snapshot

  • The use of SnapVX on the shared LVM can serve to protect against logical corruption. If there is such an occurrence, you can restore the SnapVX snapshot to the source device and roll back the logical corruption. This section covers that use case.

    Test assumptions

    To demonstrate functionality, we make the following assumptions:

    • The PowerMax device is 1EB (200 GB) and is multipath device pmax-1EB (360000970000120002165533030314542).
    • The LVM is pmax-1EB.
    • There is a single VM 103 (pmax12.prox.com) with one disk on the LVM.

    Figure 102.          VM 103 disk

    • The OS has a file /refresh/before_corruption.txt to demonstrate the pre-snapshot state.

    [root@pmax12 ~]# cd /refresh/

    [root@pmax12 refresh]# ls -l

    total 0

    -rw-r--r--. 1 root root 0 Apr 29 19:00 before_corruption.txt

    [root@pmax12 refresh]#

    • A SnapVX snapshot, before_corruption, exists that represents the state of the VM with this file.

    Step 1

    From the LVM you want to restore, copy the VM configuration files to a safe location. Dell suggests using an NFS share. You can find an example in Cloning a virtual machine to a new target cluster using SnapVX. Here, we copy the one VM file.

    root@pmax174:/# cp /etc/pve/qemu-server/103.conf /mnt/pve/vm-confs/snippets/

    Step 2

    Create a new file, after_corruption.txt, on the VM to represent the logical corruption.

    [root@pmax12 refresh]# ls -l

    total 0

    -rw-r--r--. 1 root root 0 Apr 29 19:24 after_corruption.txt

    -rw-r--r--. 1 root root 0 Apr 29 19:00 before_corruption.txt

    [root@pmax12 refresh]#

    Step 3

    Power off the VM. Delete the 103.conf file if you made a copy or move it to another directory if preferred. Do this for all VMs on the LVM. Once the conf file is removed from the /etc/pve/qemu-server directory, Proxmox will remove the VM from the UI.

    root@pmax174:/# rm /etc/pve/qemu-server/103.conf

    Figure 103.          Step 3 – LVM SnapVX restore to source

    Step 4

    Deactivate the volume group on each node.

    root@pmax174:/# vgs

      VG            #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize    VFree

      pmax-1D6        1   9   0 wz--n-   <2.00t    1.70t

      pmax-1E6        1   2   0 wz--n- <500.00g  435.98g

      pmax-1E6-copy   1   1   0 wz--n- <500.00g <468.00g

      pmax-1EB        1   1   0 wz--n- <200.00g <168.00g

      pve             1   3   0 wz--n-  277.87g   16.00g

    root@pmax174:/# vgchange -an pmax-1EB

      0 logical volume(s) in volume group "pmax-1EB" now active

    root@pmax174:/# ssh pmax172 vgchange -an pmax-1EB

      0 logical volume(s) in volume group "pmax-1EB" now active

    root@pmax174:/# ssh pmax176 vgchange -an pmax-1EB

      0 logical volume(s) in volume group "pmax-1EB" now active

    root@pmax174:/#

    Step 5

    Delete the multipath device on each node.

    root@pmax174:/# multipath -f pmax-1EB

    root@pmax174:/# ssh pmax172 multipath -f pmax-1EB

    root@pmax174:/# ssh pmax176 multipath -f pmax-1EB

    Step 6

    In Unisphere for PowerMax, unmask the device from the nodes by deleting the masking view.

    Figure 104.          Step 6 – LVM SnapVX restore to source

    Step 7

    After deleting the masking view, navigate to the storage group and click the tab Data Protection. Check the box next to the snapshot and click Restore. Click Run Now to restore the snapshot. Complete by clicking OK as in Figure 105.

    Figure 105.          Step 7 – LVM SnapVX restore to source

    Once you issue a PowerMax restore, the device is immediately available for use. PowerMax handles the copy in the background.

    Step 8

    Re-create the masking view in Unisphere for PowerMax. Since the device WWN is unchanged, you do not need to modify the alias in the multipath.conf file.

    Step 9

    Run a rescan of the devices on each Proxmox host and then the multipath commands.

    root@pmax174:/# rescan-scsi-bus.sh

    root@pmax174:/# multipath -r

    root@pmax174:/# multipath -ll

    …

    pmax-1EB (360000970000120002165533030314542) dm-13 EMC,SYMMETRIX

    size=200G features='1 queue_if_no_path' hwhandler='0' wp=rw

    `-+- policy='service-time 0' prio=1 status=active

      |- 18:0:0:4 sds 65:32 active ready running

      |- 18:0:1:4 sdt 65:48 active ready running

      |- 19:0:0:4 sdv 65:80 active ready running

      `- 19:0:1:4 sdu 65:64 active ready running

    root@pmax172:/#

    Step 10

    Run pvscan and vgscan and then activate the volume group.

    root@pmax174:/# pvscan

      PV /dev/sda3                         VG pve             lvm2 [277.87 GiB / 16.00 GiB free]

      PV /dev/mapper/pmax-1E6-part1        VG pmax-1E6        lvm2 [<500.00 GiB / 435.98 GiB free]

      PV /dev/mapper/pmax-1D6-part1        VG pmax-1D6        lvm2 [<2.00 TiB / 1.70 TiB free]

      PV /dev/mapper/pmax-1EB-part1        VG pmax-1EB        lvm2 [<200.00 GiB / <168.00 GiB free]

      PV /dev/mapper/pmax-1E6-copy-part1   VG pmax-1E6-copy   lvm2 [<500.00 GiB / <468.00 GiB free]

      Total: 5 [3.44 TiB] / in use: 5 [3.44 TiB] / in no VG: 0 [0   ]

    root@pmax174:/# vgscan

      Found volume group "pve" using metadata type lvm2

      Found volume group "pmax-1E6" using metadata type lvm2

      Found volume group "pmax-1D6" using metadata type lvm2

      Found volume group "pmax-1EB" using metadata type lvm2

      Found volume group "pmax-1E6-copy" using metadata type lvm2

    root@pmax174:/# vgchange -ay pmax-1EB

      1 logical volume(s) in volume group "pmax-1EB" now active

    root@pmax174:/#

    Log back into the Proxmox UI and the LVM should be available on all nodes with the VM disk.

    Figure 106.          Step 10 – LVM SnapVX restore to source

    Step 11

    Copy back the VM conf file to the /etc/pve/qemu-server/ directory.

    root@pmax174:/# cp /mnt/pve/vm-confs/snippets/103.conf /etc/pve/qemu-server/

    Proxmox will add the VM back.

    Figure 107.          Step 11 – LVM SnapVX restore to source

    Power on the VM and check the /refresh/ directory. The after_corruption.txt is not present. The restore is successful.

    [root@pmax12 ~]# cd /refresh

    [root@pmax12 refresh]# ls -l

    total 0

    -rw-r--r--. 1 root root 0 Apr 29 19:00 before_corruption.txt

    [root@pmax12 refresh]#

    Note: If the VM has the HA attribute, it may be in a state of “fence” after the restore. In order to power the VM on, set HA to stopped or ignored and then power on. After power on, re-enable HA.

Snapshot-as-volume-chain

  • Snapshots as volume chains implement snapshots by creating a sequence (chain) of virtual disk volumes in which each new volume records only the changes since the previous one. Instead of storing multiple points in time within a single disk, Proxmox creates a new disk for each snapshot and links it to its parent as a backing volume. This approach avoids the limitations of traditional LVM snapshots while enabling snapshot support on block storage that does not natively provide snapshot capabilities.

    You enable snapshots as volume chains by selecting Allow Snapshots as Volume-Chain when creating or editing an LVM storage definition, as shown in Figure 59. With this setting, taking a snapshot persists the current state under the snapshot’s name and starts a new volume backed by the snapshot. Once enabled, Proxmox preserves the current virtual disk state under the snapshot’s name and immediately creates a new active volume that uses the snapshot as its backing volume. The active volume records only the changes relative to its parent snapshot.

    Figure 59.    Allow Snapshots as Volume-Chain

    Each volume in the chain references its parent snapshot as a backing volume. Proxmox currently implements these snapshot volumes as thick‑provisioned LVM logical volumes, even though only changed blocks consume physical space on the underlying storage. This design deliberately avoids native LVM snapshots, which often incur heavy I/O penalties and can fail catastrophically when pre‑allocated space runs out.

    Snapshots as volume chains provide vendor‑agnostic snapshot support for any storage system that exposes block devices, including iSCSI and Fibre Channel–attached SANs such as PowerMax. Although the implementation relies on the qcow2 format, Proxmox uses qcow2 only for its ability to form backing chains, not for qcow2’s internal snapshot mechanism. Proxmox VE manages snapshot creation, deletion, and rollback entirely at the storage layer.

    The Allow Snapshots as Volume-Chain setting affects only newly created virtual disk volumes. You can toggle the option while the storage is online, but once qcow2-backed volumes exist, you cannot disable it without first removing those volumes.

    For efficient operation, the backing storage must support thin provisioning and discard (TRIM) like PowerMax. While each snapshot appears to consume the full virtual disk size from the Proxmox perspective, the underlying storage allocates space only for blocks that change.

    Unlike Proxmox’s traditional internal snapshot support—which stores multiple points in time within a single disk—snapshots as volume chains create a new delta disk for each snapshot. Every snapshot therefore results in an additional logical volume of equal nominal size, chained together through backing references rather than implemented as in-place copy-on-write snapshots.

    The snapshot support offered is not the internal snapshot support which uses the single disk with a point in time but rather the snapshot as volume chains. The difference is that when you take a snapshot on the shared LVM, Proxmox generates a new delta disk that will record any changes. Each snapshot will result in another disk of equal size, thick provisioned in the LVM.

    Note: If RAM is included with the snapshot, Proxmox creates a .raw disk for that because the qcow2 is not an appropriate format for this data.

    The basic workflow follows these steps.

    Workflow

    1. Base disk (original VM disk)
      1. This is the VM’s root disk before any snapshots.
    1. Snapshot creation
      1. When a snapshot is taken, the Proxmox renames the current volume, and it becomes read-only.
      2. A new delta volume is created for future writes.
    2. Writes always go to the newest delta
      1. Each new snapshot locks the prior state, chaining deltas together.
      2. Reads may traverse the chain if a block is not found in the newest layer.
    3. Additional snapshots
      1. Each snapshot deepens the chain. The first snapshot on the base disk converts it to read-only. Proxmox then generates a new delta 1 which is read-write for future writes. A second snapshot converts delta 1 to read-only (so now there are two read-only disks), and Proxmox generates delta 2 which is read-write. Additional snapshots continue the process. We depict the workflow in Figure 60.

    Figure 60.    Volume-chain snapshots

    1. Restore or delete
      1. Restoring a snapshot rewinds the VM to the snapshot’s read-only state.
      2. Deleting snapshots requires merging child deltas back into parent volumes. Doing this may incur more space usage.

    Restrictions

    There are some restrictions when using volume-chain snapshots.

    • The backing storage must support thin-provisioning and discard like PowerMax.
    • VMs must use the qcow2 format, not raw; however, it is important to remember that the feature uses qcow2 volume layering capability (Copy-On-Write (COW)), not qcow2’s native snapshot functionality.
    • You can only roll back to the latest snapshot. If you need to use an earlier snapshot, you must first delete the newer ones. Note that this forces the merging of data to the base image and thus significant IO.

    Other restrictions can be found in the product documentation.

    Performance

    Snapshots on shared LVM have one major drawback: performance. Each write must update the snapshot map and QEMU must manage the copy-on-write (COW) images, which slows write operations. Read operations can also take longer because the system may need to traverse multiple disks to locate the requested data. Snapshots also tend to increase fragmentation. As the number of snapshots for a VM grows, the performance impact grows with it and can add 30 to 90 percent overhead. For that reason, Proxmox does not recommend snapshots on thick LVM as a long-term solution. A more suitable use case is short-term testing, such as validating patches before deployment to production.

    Converting disk format

    Since LVM snapshots require qcow2 disks, if you enable the feature on an LVM with existing raw disks, you must convert them to qcow2 before you can snapshot the VM. The snapshot option is not displayed for VMs with raw disks. In Figure 61, VM 105 has a single raw disk. Note that in the inset, Proxmox indicates that the guest configuration does not support taking snapshots.

    Figure 61.    LVM with snapshots enabled

    You can convert to qcow2 online or offline. In this example, the VM is running. Highlight the Hard Disk and use the drop-down menu under Disk Action to choose Move Storage, as in Figure 62. Select the Target Storage, which is the same LVM, but under Format, choose qcow2. Proxmox will clone the disk, so use the checkbox (hidden) to enable deletion of the source if desired.

    Figure 62.    Move raw to qcow2

    The Task viewer displays the progress. The time to complete is dependent on the disk size.

    Figure 63.    Task viewer of qcow2 conversion

    After the conversion completes, the warning is gone and the Take Snapshot button becomes available.

    Figure 64.    Snapshot functionality post-qcow2 conversion

    Using snapshots

    Taking a snapshot in the Proxmox UI is the same for LVM as it is for LVM-thin. The following section details taking and restoring a snapshot, as well as shares details on the snapshot files.

    Step 1

    We navigate in the Proxmox UI to VM 105 from the previous section. The VM has a single disk on the PMAX-1E6 LVM shared storage.

    Figure 65.    Step 1 – Snapshot management

    This disk is the only one showing in the LVM.

    Figure 66.    Step 1 – Snapshot management

    Step 2

    Highlight the Snapshots menu option for VM 105. Click Take Snapshot.

    Figure 67.    Step 2 – Snapshot management

    Step 3

    Enter a Name and, if desired, Description. We will not include RAM in the first snapshot. Click Take Snapshot.

    Figure 68.    Step 3 – Snapshot management

    The Task viewer shows the steps. Note that Proxmox renames the base disk since it is now read-only and then creates a new disk for future writes. This is in line with the previous explanation in Figure 60.

    Figure 69.    Step 3 – Snapshot management

    If you view the LVM storage, you will see only the original disk, which is in fact the new delta disk.

    Figure 70.    Step 3 – Snapshot management

    Step 4

    Take a second snapshot, this time with RAM.

    Figure 71.    Step 4 – Snapshot management

    Now, if you view the LVM, there is a second file for the RAM. Note the format is raw, not qcow2.

    Figure 72.    Step 4 – Snapshot management

    Though the LVM does not show the renamed read-only disks in the UI, they are present if you query the lvs on the node.

    root@pmax174:~# lvs|grep 105

      snap_vm-105-disk-0_First_snapshot.qcow2  pmax-1E6 -wi-ao----   <32.01g

      snap_vm-105-disk-0_Second_snapshot.qcow2 pmax-1E6 -wi-ao----   <32.01g

      vm-105-disk-0.qcow2                      pmax-1E6 -wi-ao----   <32.01g

      vm-105-state-Second_snapshot             pmax-1E6 -wi-------   <8.49g

    Step 5

    Next, attempt to restore the First_snapshot by highlighting the snapshot in the UI and clicking Rollback. Then click Yes.

    Figure 73.    Step 5 – Snapshot management

    If you attempt this, you will receive the following error message because you cannot jump snapshots for restores.

    Figure 74.    Step 5 – Snapshot management

    Step 6

    Now we delete Second_snapshot so we can restore to the First_snapshot.

    Figure 75.    Step 6 – Snapshot management

    In the Task viewer output, we can see how it creates a new file that points to the First_snapshot file as the new backing file or source of truth.

    Renamed "vm-105-disk-0.qcow2" to "del-vm-105-disk-0.qcow2" in volume group "pmax-1E6"
      Rounding up size to full physical extent <32.01 GiB
      Logical volume "vm-105-disk-0.qcow2" created.
    Formatting '/dev/pmax-1E6/vm-105-disk-0.qcow2', fmt=qcow2 cluster_size=131072 extended_l2=on preallocation=metadata compression_type=zlib size=34359738368 backing_file=snap_vm-105-disk-0_First_snapshot.qcow2 backing_fmt=qcow2 lazy_refcounts=off refcount_bits=16
    TASK OK

    After the rollback, HA restarts the VM.

Solutions Enabler

  • Solutions Enabler (SE) is a powerful command-line interface (CLI) tool designed for managing, automating, and monitoring Dell PowerMax storage systems. It provides granular control over a wide range of storage operations, including those that are unavailable in Unisphere for PowerMax. SE is especially well-suited for advanced users who require scriptable, dependable, and automation-friendly interfaces for enterprise-scale storage environments. Administrators can use SE to provision storage, manage replication (including SRDF and SnapVX), configure access control via masking views, and pull real-time performance and health metrics.

    Installed on a Windows, Linux, or UNIX management host, SE can communicate with arrays using either in-band (via HBA) or out-of-band (over IP) connections. It is frequently used in automated workflows, batch jobs, and integrations with orchestration platforms such as Ansible.

Summary

  • This paper demonstrates that Proxmox Virtual Environment 9 integrates effectively with Dell PowerMax to deliver a shared, enterprise‑class virtualization platform without requiring a hyperconverged storage model. By combining a Proxmox VE cluster with PowerMax Fibre Channel block storage and optional NFS file services, the solution provides consistent shared access to virtual machine and container data while enabling key capabilities such as live migration, high availability, and centralized storage management.

    The documented implementation shows how PowerMax service levels, multipathing, and thick‑provisioned LVM storage align well with Proxmox workloads, providing predictable performance and operational simplicity. Native PowerMax SnapVX snapshots extend data protection beyond hypervisor‑level mechanisms, allowing administrators to create reusable VM copies and perform restores with minimal disruption and without the performance penalties associated with VM‑centric snapshot methods. The paper also clarifies where Proxmox shared‑LVM snapshot functionality fits, highlighting its limitations and reinforcing SnapVX as the preferred enterprise snapshot solution in this architecture.

    With the addition of Proxmox Datacenter Manager, the solution scales beyond a single cluster, enabling centralized visibility and cross‑cluster VM migration while preserving individual cluster autonomy. Operational workflows such as provisioning, monitoring, recovery, and migration remain clear and repeatable, making the platform well suited for production environments that demand reliability, performance isolation, and flexible growth.

    Overall, implementing Proxmox 9 on Dell PowerMax offers organizations a robust alternative to hyperconverged designs, combining an open virtualization platform with proven enterprise storage capabilities. This architecture enables administrators to modernize virtualization infrastructure while continuing to leverage PowerMax data services, operational maturity, and scale for mission‑critical workloads.

Terminology

  • The following table provides definitions for some of the terms in this document.

    Table 1.      Terminology

    Term

    Definition

    FC

    Fibre Channel

    HA

    High Availability; Proxmox functionality that automatically restarts virtual machines on surviving cluster nodes after a failure.

    Live migration

    The process of moving a running virtual machine from one Proxmox node to another without guest downtime, requiring shared storage.

    LVM

    Logical Volume Manager; a Linux disk management framework used by Proxmox for block‑based storage pools. LVM will always refer to thick LVM, not thin which is LVM-Thin.

    Masking View

    A PowerMax construct that controls which hosts can access specific storage devices.

    Multipathing (DM‑Multipath)

    A Linux framework that provides path redundancy and load balancing for block devices connected through multiple storage paths.

    NFS

    Network File System

    NIC

    Network Interface Controller

    Proxmox Datacenter Manager

    A centralized management component that provides visibility and operational control across multiple Proxmox VE clusters. The document uses the term Datacenter Manager without the Proxmox prefix.

    Proxmox VE

    An open‑source virtualization platform based on KVM and Linux containers, providing clustering, HA, and integrated storage management.

    pvscan

    Linux physical volume scan

    qcow2

    A virtual disk format that supports features such as snapshots and compression, with additional runtime overhead compared to raw disks.

    Raw disk

    A virtual disk format that maps directly to underlying storage with minimal overhead and no native snapshot support.

    SnapVX

    Dell PowerMax snapshot technology that provides space‑efficient point‑in‑time copies of volumes.

    Solutions Enabler (SE)

    A command‑line management toolkit used to configure, automate, and monitor PowerMax storage systems.

    SRDF

    Symmetrix Remote Data Facility

    SRP

    Storage Resource Pool

    TimeFinder

    The PowerMax local replication framework that includes SnapVX and clone technologies. The term is not always included when referring to the technology.

    Unisphere for PowerMax

    A web‑based management interface for provisioning, monitoring, and managing PowerMax storage systems.

    vgimportclone

    Linux LVM import when a duplicate exists

    vgscan

    Linux volume group scan

    VM

    Virtual Machine

    WWN

    World Wide Name; a unique identifier used in Fibre Channel storage environments to identify hosts and storage ports.

Unisphere for PowerMax

  • Unisphere for PowerMax is an HTML5 web-based application that enables you to provision, operate and maintain PowerMax, VMAX All Flash, and VMAX storage systems.

    Unisphere for PowerMax 10.4.0.x supports:

    • Storage systems (PowerMax 2500 and PowerMax 8500) running PowerMaxOS 10 (6079)
    • Storage systems (PowerMax 2000, PowerMax 8000, VMAX 250F, VMAX 450F, VMAX 850F, and VMAX 950F) running PowerMaxOS 5978
    • Storage systems (VMAX 100K, VMAX 200K, VMAX 400K, VMAX 250F, VMAX 450F, VMAX 850F, and VMAX 950F) running HYPERMAX OS 5977

    Unisphere for PowerMax has a built-in Representational State Transfer (REST). The REST API allows you to access diagnostic, performance, and configuration data, as well as perform provisioning operations on the storage system through interfaces like the CSI driver. Full documentation for the Unisphere for PowerMax REST API is available at https://developer.dell.com/ or from the Help menu within the Unisphere for PowerMax User Interface.

Virtual Machine

  • You can use either CLI (qm) or the UI to deploy a VM. To create a VM using the UI, follow these steps.

    Step 1

    Navigate to Datacenter (<your cluster>) in the left-hand menu and then click Create VM in the right-hand top menu.

    Figure 42.    Step 1 – VM creation

    Step 2

    In the General screen both Node and VM ID will default. You can change either or both if desired. Enter a Name. The other fields are optional. Click Next.

    Figure 43.    Step 2 – VM creation

    Step 3

    In the OS tab, use the drop-downs to select Storage and ISO image. You will only see storage that can store ISO images. The Type and Version default. Click Next.

    Figure 44.    Step 3 – VM creation

    Step 4

    Leave the System tab as default. In the Disks tab, use the drop-downs to select the Storage and Disk size. The Format drop-down will show the available types based on the storage selection. In this example, the storage is a shared LVM with snapshots enabled so any format is possible. Adjust other optional items as desired and click Next.

    Figure 45.    Step 4 – VM creation

    Step 5

    Make changes to the CPU, Memory, and Network tabs. In the Confirm tab, review, and click Finish below. The VM powers on by default.

    Figure 46.    Step 5 – VM creation

    The installation then starts up.

    Figure 47.    VM installation
